intro.text: The New Testament uses the name Herod for three men: the king of Matthew 2 and Luke 1, the tetrarch of the Gospels and Acts 13:1, and the king of Acts 12. It names three more rulers of the family: Archelaus, Philip the tetrarch and King Agrippa.

Scripture states only three family links among them: Archelaus reigned "in the room of his father Herod"; Philip was the tetrarch's brother; and Herodias had been "his brother Philip's wife". The rest of the family tree comes from Josephus.

Josephus, a Jewish historian of the first century, is the main outside source. He wrote the Jewish War late in Vespasian's reign (AD 69–79) and finished the Antiquities in AD 93 or 94 (Schürer, 1890). He is quoted here in William Whiston's translation of 1737, with the book, chapter and section numbers of the project's copy.

Dates are reconstructions. These pages give Schürer's (1890): Herod the Great king 37–4 BC; Archelaus 4 BC – AD 6; Antipas 4 BC – AD 39; Philip 4 BC – AD 34; Agrippa I AD 37–44; Agrippa II about AD 50–100. Other views are shown on each page.

Scripture gives none of these men a regnal verdict. Each page shows what the text says of him, quoted as it stands; for four of them, that means their dealings with Jesus, John the Baptist, the apostles or Paul.

rulers.name: Herod the Great
rulers.title: King of Judaea, under Rome
rulers.tagline: King in Jerusalem when Jesus was born in Bethlehem.

capital.name: Jerusalem
capital.note: Matthew finds him in Jerusalem, where "all Jerusalem" was troubled with him.

identifications.text: Matthew calls him only "Herod the king" and Luke "Herod, the king of Judaea". Matthew ties him to the rest of the family in one phrase: Archelaus reigned "in the room of his father Herod".

Luke's "Herod, the king of Judaea" is set before the births of John and Jesus. Schürer (1890) notes that Luke 1:5, like Matthew 2, assumes the birth fell in Herod's lifetime; Archelaus was not made king, and Agrippa I ruled Judaea only from AD 41.
Josephus tells of Herod son of Antipater, whom Rome made king of Judaea and who left Judaea to his son Archelaus (Antiquities 14.14.4–5; 17.8.1; 17.11.4).
Schürer (1890) notes that the name "the Great" is used by Josephus in a single passage (Antiquities 18.5.4); Scripture never uses it.

"Herod's judgment hall" at Caesarea, where Paul was kept, is taken by commentators to be the palace Herod the Great had built there and the governors later used (Poole, 1683; Meyer, English translation 1877–1879; Vincent, 1887). Acts does not say which Herod built it.

reign.text: Not given in Scripture: Jesus was born "in the days of Herod the king", and the family stayed in Egypt "until the death of Herod".

dates.label: Scripture's numbers
dates.note: None. Matthew and Luke date events by his reign (Matthew 2:1; Luke 1:5) but give no years.

dates.label: Schürer (1890)
dates.note: Made king by the Roman Senate late in 40 BC; took Jerusalem in 37 BC; died at Jericho shortly before the Passover of 4 BC.

dates.label: Josephus's own count
dates.note: "Having reigned, since he had procured Antigonus to be slain, thirty-four years; but since he had been declared king by the Romans, thirty-seven" (Antiquities 17.8.1; also War 1.33.8).

dates.label: A later death: 3 BC or 1 BC (minority, as listed by Schürer)
dates.note: Quandt and Kellner put his death in 3 BC; Caspari and Riess in 1 BC (Schürer, 1890, p. 466, lists them without their reasons).

scriptureSays.text: Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judaea "in the days of Herod the king", when wise men came from the east to Jerusalem asking, "Where is he that is born King of the Jews?"

"When Herod the king had heard these things, he was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him." He asked the chief priests and scribes where Christ should be born, and they answered, "In Bethlehem of Judaea."
He called the wise men privately, "enquired of them diligently what time the star appeared", and sent them to Bethlehem: "bring me word again, that I may come and worship him also."
Warned of God in a dream, the wise men did not return to Herod. An angel told Joseph, "Herod will seek the young child to destroy him", and the family fled into Egypt "until the death of Herod".

When he saw that he was mocked, he "was exceeding wroth" and "slew all the children that were in Bethlehem, and in all the coasts thereof, from two years old and under", reckoning by the time the wise men had given him.
"But when Herod was dead", Matthew says, an angel of the Lord appeared in a dream to Joseph in Egypt: "they are dead which sought the young child's life."
Luke dates the angel's announcement to Zacharias "in the days of Herod, the king of Judaea".
Scripture gives Herod no regnal record: no length of reign, no verdict formula, no burial. Everything it says of him belongs to the accounts of the births of John the Baptist and Jesus.

accession.text: Josephus says the Roman Senate, on the motion of Antony and with Octavian ("Caesar") in favour, decreed that Herod should be king, while Antigonus held Jerusalem with Parthian support (Antiquities 14.14.4).
Schürer (1890) dates the appointment to the end of 40 BC, from the consuls Josephus names.

Herod and the Roman general Sosius took Jerusalem; Antigonus was sent in bonds to Antony, and Herod gave Antony money to have him slain, "and thus did the government of the Asamoneans cease" (Antiquities 14.16.4).
Josephus reports that Antigonus, before the walls, called Herod "a private man, and an Idumean, i.e. a half Jew" (Antiquities 14.15.2).
After Antony's defeat, Herod met Octavian, who "restored him his diadem again" (Antiquities 15.6.7).

claim.text: The Senate in Rome decreed Herod king of Judaea, and he went up to the Capitol between Antony and Octavian (Antiquities 14.14.4–5).
Herod and Sosius took Jerusalem; Antigonus was carried off to Antony (Antiquities 14.16.4).
He built a harbour city at Strato's Tower and called it Caesarea; Josephus says it was finished in twelve years (Antiquities 15.9.6).
He began to rebuild the temple, "in the eighteenth year of his reign" by the Antiquities (15.11.1), "in the fifteenth year" by the War (1.21.1).
Alexander and Aristobulus, his sons by Mariamne, were strangled at Sebaste by their father's command (Antiquities 16.11.7).
Wise men from the east came to Jerusalem; Herod sent them to Bethlehem.
He slew the children of Bethlehem and its coasts, from two years old and under.
At Jericho, near death, he had his son Antipater killed, and died five days later (Antiquities 17.7.1; 17.8.1).
His body was carried in procession toward Herodium, "for there by his own command he was to be buried" (Antiquities 17.8.3).

worship.text: Herod gathered "all the chief priests and scribes of the people" to ask where Christ should be born.
The temple of Jesus' day had been "Forty and six years" in building, the Jews said to Jesus at Jerusalem. John does not name the builder.

Schürer (1890) dates the start of Herod's rebuilding to the end of 20 or the beginning of 19 BC; counting the forty-six years from then, he places that Passover of John 2 in AD 27 or, "more probably", AD 28.

building.text: Josephus credits him with Caesarea's harbour, theatre and amphitheatre (Antiquities 15.9.6), the rebuilt temple and its cloisters, the fortress he named Antonia and a palace in the upper city (War 1.21.1).
Schürer (1890) takes the Antiquities' eighteenth year, 20/19 BC, for the start of the temple work, and suggests the War's fifteenth year is wrong or counts the preparations.

alliances.text: He held his kingdom from Rome: from Antony and the Senate first, then from Octavian, whom he supplied on the march to Egypt (Antiquities 14.14.4; 15.6.7).
His will left gifts to Caesar and to Caesar's wife Julia (Antiquities 17.8.1).

people.text: "All Jerusalem" was troubled with him at the wise men's question.
Matthew sets Jeremiah's words of Rachel weeping in Rama beside the slaughter at Bethlehem.

Josephus says that, dying at Jericho, he ordered the principal men of the nation shut in the hippodrome and killed at his death, so that the nation would mourn (Antiquities 17.6.5); his sister Salome released them instead (War 1.33.8).

person.name: Micah
person.note: Matthew says only "the prophet"; the words are those of Micah 5:2.

claim.text: The chief priests and scribes answered Herod's question from "the prophet": out of Bethlehem "shall come a Governor, that shall rule my people Israel".

quote.text: And thou Bethlehem, in the land of Juda, art not the least among the princes of Juda: for out of thee shall come a Governor, that shall rule my people Israel.

claim.text: Matthew says the slaughter at Bethlehem fulfilled what was "spoken by Jeremy the prophet".

quote.text: In Rama was there a voice heard, lamentation, and weeping, and great mourning, Rachel weeping for her children, and would not be comforted, because they are not.

claim.text: Herod was made king on Antony's motion with Octavian's support (Antiquities 14.14.4) and kept his crown under Octavian, "Caesar" in Josephus (Antiquities 15.6.7), who later took the name Augustus.

rulers.name: Antigonus
rulers.note: the last Hasmonean king, set up with Parthian help

claim.text: Antigonus, whom Herod displaced, held the kingdom with Parthian backing; Josephus has him speak of being deprived of it "as having received it from the Parthians" (Antiquities 14.15.2).

Schürer (1890) names Josephus's Antiquities 15–17 and War 1 as the sources for Herod's reign; Josephus wrote the War late in Vespasian's reign and finished the Antiquities in AD 93 or 94. Josephus tells the reign at length but does not mention the wise men or the children of Bethlehem, a silence Barnes (1832) and Strauss (1846) both discuss.

Josephus notes that on the night Herod burned "the other Matthias, who had raised the sedition, with his companions, alive", "there was an eclipse of the moon" (Antiquities 17.6.4). Its date is discussed under the question of when Herod died.

outside.name: Macrobius, Saturnalia 2.4.11
outside.date: written about four centuries after Herod

claim.text: A Latin writer, Macrobius, tells that Augustus, hearing that among the boys under two years old whom Herod king of the Jews ordered killed in Syria his own son had also been killed, said: "It is better to be Herod's pig than his son" (our translation of the Latin).
Eusebius quotes Josephus's account of Herod's last illness and calls it "a just punishment for his slaughter of the children of Bethlehem" (Church History 1.8.16).

twoAccounts.topic: The temple: when the rebuilding began

first.text: The War: "in the fifteenth year of his reign, Herod rebuilt the temple" (1.21.1).

second.text: The Antiquities: "in the eighteenth year of his reign" (15.11.1).

first.text: Matthew says only that Herod died while the family was in Egypt: "But when Herod was dead".

second.text: Josephus tells a long illness, the baths at Callirrhoe, the killing of Antipater, and death at Jericho five days later (Antiquities 17.6.5; 17.7.1; 17.8.1).

views.label: 4 BC, shortly before the Passover
views.holders: Schürer (1890), with Fréret, Sanclemente, Ideler, Wieseler and most scholars he lists

argument.text: Josephus counts 34 years from Jerusalem's capture (37 BC) and 37 from the appointment (40 BC), counting part-years as years; the eclipse of 12–13 March 4 BC precedes the death; and his sons' reigns count from 4 BC (Archelaus deposed in AD 6 in his tenth year; Antipas's coins reach his forty-third year in AD 39).

views.label: 3 BC
views.holders: Quandt and Kellner, as listed by Schürer (1890)

argument.text: Schürer names them as placing the death a year later; he does not set out their reasons.

views.label: 1 BC
views.holders: Caspari and Riess (1880), as listed by Schürer (1890)

argument.text: Schürer names them as diverging further, to 1 BC (and Seyffarth further still, to AD 1); he does not set out their reasons.

questions.question: Herod's death and the date of Jesus' birth

views.label: In Herod's last years; Luke's Quirinius is a mistake
views.holders: Schürer (1890)

argument.text: Schürer notes that Luke 1:5, as well as Matthew 2, assumes Jesus was born in Herod's lifetime. But Quirinius was not governor of Syria in Herod's last years, so Schürer holds that Luke's census (Luke 2:2) cannot belong to Herod's reign.

views.label: About 6 BC, at an enrolment held under Herod
views.holders: W. M. Ramsay (1898)

argument.text: Ramsay argues that the first periodic enrolment of Syria was made in 8–7 BC, that Palestine's was delayed to the late summer or autumn of 6 BC, and that Quirinius then commanded Syria's armies; Jesus was born then.

questions.question: Why does no other ancient record tell of the children of Bethlehem?

views.label: Silence is no argument
views.holders: Albert Barnes (1832)

argument.text: Barnes gives three reasons for Josephus's silence: a Jewish historian would not record what seemed to confirm Christianity; the deed was small beside Herod's other crimes, Bethlehem being a small village; and the order may have been secret.

views.label: Macrobius remembers it
views.holders: John Gill (1746–1748); F. W. Farrar (1874, quoted in the Pulpit Commentary); W. M. Ramsay (1898)

argument.text: They read Macrobius's story as a mixed or dim memory of the slaughter. Ramsay thinks Macrobius did not take it from a Christian writer, because a Christian would have said Palestine, not Syria.

views.label: The silence counts against the story
views.holders: D. F. Strauss (1835; English 1846)

argument.text: Strauss holds that so unprecedented a massacre would be noticed by Josephus and the rabbis, and that Macrobius's passage "loses all credit" by confusing the infants with Herod's grown son Antipater.

notSaid: Scripture never calls him "the Great".
Scripture gives no length of reign, no verdict formula and no burial for Herod.
Matthew does not say how many children died at Bethlehem.
Scripture does not say how Herod died or where he was buried.
The Gospels do not say who rebuilt the temple of Jesus' day; John 2:20 gives only its forty-six years of building.
Matthew does not say how long after the birth the wise men came; Herod's "two years old and under" is reckoned from the time of the star.

places.name: Jerusalem
places.note: Where the wise men came and Herod questioned them

places.name: Bethlehem
places.note: Jesus' birthplace; the children slain

places.name: Egypt
places.note: Where the family fled until Herod's death

places.name: Ramah
places.note: Named in the words of Jeremiah that Matthew quotes

places.name: Jericho
places.note: Where he died, by Josephus (Antiquities 17.6.5; 17.8.1)

places.name: Caesarea
places.note: The city he built (Josephus); "Herod's judgment hall" there

places.name: Herodium
places.note: His burial place, by Josephus (Antiquities 17.8.3); not in the atlas

rulers.name: Archelaus
rulers.title: Ruler of Judaea under Rome (ethnarch, by Josephus)
rulers.tagline: The son whose rule in Judaea turned Joseph aside to Galilee.

capital.name: Jerusalem
capital.note: Scripture names only Judaea (Matthew 2:22); Jerusalem by Josephus

identifications.text: Matthew names him once, as son of Herod: "Archelaus did reign in Judaea in the room of his father Herod".

Josephus: Herod's last will made Archelaus king; Augustus made him instead "ethnarch of the one half" of Herod's kingdom, Judaea, Samaria and Idumaea, and promised him the royal dignity later if he governed well (Antiquities 17.8.1; 17.11.4).
Schürer (1890) assigns him the coins inscribed, in Greek, "of Herod the ethnarch", since no other Herodian bore that title, and notes that the Roman historian Dio Cassius calls him Herod.

reign.text: Not given in Scripture: Matthew says only that he "did reign in Judaea in the room of his father Herod".

dates.label: Schürer (1890)
dates.note: Ethnarch from Herod's death in 4 BC until Augustus deposed him and banished him to Vienne in Gaul in AD 6.

dates.label: Josephus's two counts
dates.note: Banished "in the tenth year of Archelaus's government" (Antiquities 17.13.2) or "in the ninth year" (War 2.7.3). Schürer takes the tenth, with Dio Cassius's date of AD 6.

scriptureSays.text: "When he heard that Archelaus did reign in Judaea in the room of his father Herod, he was afraid to go thither": Joseph, warned in a dream, turned aside into Galilee.
Joseph settled the family in "a city called Nazareth".
This is the only verse that names Archelaus. Scripture records nothing he did or said.

accession.text: Herod's final will named Archelaus king and his brother Antipas tetrarch (Antiquities 17.8.1).
Before sailing for Rome to have the will confirmed, Archelaus sent his army against a Passover crowd in the temple; Josephus says the horsemen "slew three thousand men" (Antiquities 17.9.3).
In Rome an embassy of fifty Jews, joined by more than eight thousand Jews living there, asked Augustus to let them live by their own laws rather than under Archelaus (Antiquities 17.11.1).
Augustus made him ethnarch, "not indeed to be king of the whole country", and divided the rest between Antipas and Philip (Antiquities 17.11.4).

claim.text: At the Passover his army fell on those gathered at the temple; his horsemen killed three thousand (Antiquities 17.9.3).
Fifty envoys pleaded against him before Augustus (Antiquities 17.11.1).
Augustus gave him half of Herod's kingdom as ethnarch (Antiquities 17.11.4).
Afraid of Archelaus, Joseph took the child and his mother to Galilee and Nazareth.
He rebuilt the royal palace at Jericho, watered new palm groves and founded a village he named Archelais (Antiquities 17.13.1).
Accused by "both his brethren, and the principal men of Judea and Samaria", he was banished by Caesar to Vienne in Gaul and his money taken (Antiquities 17.13.2).

worship.text: He removed and appointed high priests: Joazar, then his brother Eleazar, then Jesus son of Sie (Antiquities 17.13.1).
Josephus says he "transgressed the law of our fathers" by marrying Glaphyra, the widow of his brother Alexander, who had children by her (Antiquities 17.13.1).

building.text: The Jericho palace, the palm groves and the village of Archelais (Antiquities 17.13.1).

alliances.text: He ruled only by Augustus's grant and was removed by Augustus (Antiquities 17.11.4; 17.13.2).

people.text: Josephus says the Jews and Samaritans both sent ambassadors against him to Caesar (War 2.7.3).
After his banishment his territory was added to the province of Syria, and Cyrenius came to take an account of the people's property (Antiquities 18.1.1).

claim.text: Augustus confirmed only part of Herod's will, made Archelaus ethnarch, and ten years later banished him (Antiquities 17.11.4; 17.13.2).
When Archelaus was gone, his country "was now added to the province of Syria" and Cyrenius came to tax it (Antiquities 18.1.1).

Josephus is the only full outside account of Archelaus: the Passover slaughter, the hearing before Augustus, the marriage to Glaphyra, a dream of nine ears of corn, and the banishment (Antiquities 17.9–13; War 2.7.3).

first.text: Matthew: "Archelaus did reign in Judaea in the room of his father Herod."

second.text: Josephus: Augustus made him "not indeed to be king of the whole country, but ethnarch of the one half" (Antiquities 17.11.4); yet elsewhere Josephus himself calls him "his son Archelaus, who was made king after him" (Antiquities 18.4.3).

first.text: War 2.7.3: "in the ninth year of his government he was banished to Vienna, a city of Gaul".

second.text: Antiquities 17.13.2: "in the tenth year of Archelaus's government".

questions.question: Is Archelaus behind Jesus' parable of the nobleman (Luke 19:12–27)?

views.label: Yes, the story echoes his journey to Rome
views.holders: H. A. W. Meyer (English 1880); F. W. Farrar (1880); C. J. Ellicott's commentary (about 1880); A. B. Bruce (1897), who says the idea has been "very generally accepted" since Clericus and Wolf

argument.text: A nobleman goes "into a far country to receive for himself a kingdom" and his citizens send after him, "We will not have this man to reign over us". They compare Archelaus's journey to Augustus and the embassy of fifty sent against him (Antiquities 17.11.1); Farrar notes that Herod and Archelaus had both gone from Jericho to Rome to receive a kingdom, and Jesus told the parable near Jericho (Luke 19:1, 11).

views.label: Jesus would not have pictured himself by Archelaus
views.holders: Schanz, as reported by A. B. Bruce (1897), who disagrees

argument.text: Bruce reports Schanz's objection that Jesus would not choose so bad a man to stand for himself, and answers that Jesus also used an unjust judge and an unjust steward in parables.

notSaid: Scripture names Archelaus once (Matthew 2:22) and records nothing he did.
Scripture does not call him king or ethnarch; it says he "did reign".
Scripture does not record his removal by Augustus.
Luke's parable of the nobleman (Luke 19:12) names no ruler.

places.name: Judaea
places.note: Where he reigned

places.name: Galilee
places.note: Where Joseph turned aside

places.name: Nazareth
places.note: Where the family settled

places.name: Jerusalem
places.note: The Passover slaughter in the temple, by Josephus (Antiquities 17.9.3)

places.name: Jericho
places.note: His rebuilt palace, by Josephus (Antiquities 17.13.1)

places.name: Vienne, in Gaul
places.note: His place of banishment, by Josephus (Antiquities 17.13.2); not in the atlas

rulers.name: Herod Antipas
rulers.title: Tetrarch of Galilee and Perea, under Rome
rulers.tagline: The tetrarch who beheaded John the Baptist and questioned Jesus.

capital.name: Tiberias
capital.note: The city he built on the lake and named for Tiberius (Josephus, Antiquities 18.2.3)

identifications.text: The Gospels and Acts call him "Herod the tetrarch", and Luke "tetrarch of Galilee"; Luke names Philip as his brother. Scripture never uses the name Antipas.

Josephus calls Herod's son Antipas tetrarch of Galilee and Perea, and often names him, as the Gospels do, "Herod the tetrarch": the one who married Herodias and put John the Baptist to death (Antiquities 17.8.1; 18.2.3; 18.5.1–2).
Schürer (1890) notes that Antipas is the only man called Herod who bore the title of tetrarch (his brother Philip was also a tetrarch, but is never called Herod).
The Herod of Jesus' trial is the same man: Pilate sent Jesus to him on learning that he was a Galilean and "belonged unto Herod's jurisdiction". Acts 4:27 looks back on that day.

Three verses say only "Herod": Jesus' warning about "the leaven of Herod", Joanna "the wife of Chuza Herod's steward", and the Pharisees' "Herod will kill thee". They are taken as the tetrarch from their setting: Jesus' work in Galilee and on the road, after "Herod was dead" (Matthew 2:19) and before the "Herod the king" of Acts 12.

The dancer is called only "the daughter of Herodias". Josephus names Herodias's daughter Salome, later the wife of Philip the tetrarch (Antiquities 18.5.4); Schürer (1890) takes her to be the dancer. The site's person record for her (Salome) rests on that identification.

reign.text: Not given in Scripture: Luke places him as "tetrarch of Galilee" in the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar.

dates.label: Schürer (1890)
dates.note: Tetrarch from Herod's death in 4 BC until Gaius (Caligula) deposed him, in the summer of AD 39 by Schürer's reckoning; his coins run to the forty-third year of his rule.

dates.label: Josephus
dates.note: No length of rule. Gaius "took away from him his tetrarchy" and banished him to Lyons (Antiquities 18.7.2).

scriptureSays.text: John the Baptist reproved "Herod the tetrarch" "for Herodias his brother Philip's wife, and for all the evils which Herod had done", and Herod "shut up John in prison".
John had told him, "It is not lawful for thee to have thy brother's wife." Matthew says Herod would have put him to death but "feared the multitude, because they counted him as a prophet".
Mark says Herodias wanted John dead, "but she could not: For Herod feared John, knowing that he was a just man and an holy", and "heard him gladly".

At his birthday supper the daughter of Herodias danced; he swore to give her whatever she asked, "unto the half of my kingdom". Prompted by her mother she asked for "the head of John the Baptist". "The king was exceeding sorry; yet for his oath's sake" he sent and had John beheaded in the prison.

Hearing of Jesus' works, he said, "It is John, whom I beheaded: he is risen from the dead." In Luke he is "perplexed": "John have I beheaded: but who is this, of whom I hear such things? And he desired to see him."
Some Pharisees warned Jesus, "Herod will kill thee." Jesus answered, "Go ye, and tell that fox, Behold, I cast out devils, and I do cures to day and to morrow".
Jesus warned his disciples to "beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, and of the leaven of Herod".

At the trial Pilate sent Jesus to Herod, who "was exceeding glad" and "hoped to have seen some miracle done by him". He questioned him "in many words; but he answered him nothing". Herod and his soldiers "set him at nought, and mocked him, and arrayed him in a gorgeous robe", and sent him back.
"The same day Pilate and Herod were made friends together." Pilate told the accusers, "No, nor yet Herod" had found anything worthy of death in Jesus.
The church in Jerusalem said in prayer that "both Herod, and Pontius Pilate, with the Gentiles, and the people of Israel, were gathered together" against Jesus.
Among those near him: Joanna, "the wife of Chuza Herod's steward", who ministered to Jesus; and Manaen of the church at Antioch, "brought up with Herod the tetrarch".

accession.text: Herod's last will made Antipas "tetrarch of Galilee and Perea" (Antiquities 17.8.1).
Augustus confirmed it: "to him it was that Peres and Galilee paid their tribute, which amounted annually to two hundred talents" (Antiquities 17.11.4).

claim.text: He walled Sepphoris, "the security of all Galilee", and Betharamphtha, which he named Julias after the emperor's wife (Antiquities 18.2.1).
He built Tiberias on the lake, "in great favor with Tiberius", on ground where graves had to be removed (Antiquities 18.2.3).
He married Herodias, "his brother Philip's wife".
He shut up John in prison after John reproved him.
At his birthday supper he granted the head of John the Baptist.
He thought John had risen, and desired to see Jesus.
Warned that Herod would kill him, Jesus sent word to "that fox".
At Jerusalem he questioned and mocked Jesus and sent him back to Pilate.

Aretas's daughter fled to her father on learning that Antipas meant to divorce her for Herodias; war followed over that and a border dispute, and "all Herod's army was destroyed" (Antiquities 18.5.1).
Urged by Herodias to seek a royal title, he went to Gaius, was accused by Agrippa, lost his tetrarchy and was banished to Lyons; Herodias went with him (Antiquities 18.7.1–2).

worship.text: He was in Jerusalem at the Passover of Jesus' trial: "who himself also was at Jerusalem at that time".
Josephus says that building Tiberias over graves was "to transgress the Jewish ancient laws", since such inhabitants were unclean for seven days (Antiquities 18.2.3).

alliances.text: His first wife was the daughter of Aretas, king of Arabia; she fled to her father when she learned he had agreed to divorce her for Herodias, and Aretas made it "the first occasion of his enmity" (Antiquities 18.5.1).
Before the trial Pilate and he "were at enmity between themselves"; that day they became friends.

people.text: His birthday supper was for "his lords, high captains, and chief estates of Galilee".

Josephus: "some of the Jews thought that the destruction of Herod's army came from God, and that very justly, as a punishment of what he did against John, that was called the Baptist" (Antiquities 18.5.2).
He peopled Tiberias partly by force: strangers, Galileans, poor people and freed slaves (Antiquities 18.2.3).

claim.text: John reproved him over Herodias "and for all the evils which Herod had done", and was imprisoned and beheaded for it.

quote.text: It is not lawful for thee to have her.

claim.text: Augustus gave him Galilee and Perea (Antiquities 17.11.4); he named Tiberias for Tiberius, with whom he stood "in great favor" (18.2.3); Gaius banished him (18.7.2).
Pilate sent Jesus to him and he sent Jesus back; "the same day Pilate and Herod were made friends together".

rulers.name: Aretas
rulers.note: Aretas IV; Schürer (1890) takes the Aretas of 2 Corinthians 11:32 to be the same king

claim.text: Schürer (1890) dates Aretas IV from 9 BC to AD 40, puts his war with Antipas in AD 36, and identifies him with the King Aretas whose governor held Damascus when Paul escaped (2 Corinthians 11:32).

Josephus calls John "a good man" who "commanded the Jews to exercise virtue" and "to come to baptism"; Herod, fearing "lest the great influence John had over the people might put it into his power and inclination to raise a rebellion", sent him prisoner to Macherus, "and was there put to death".

outside.name: Whether the John passage is genuine

claim.text: Schürer (1890) uses the passage, "if it really belongs originally to him", but adds that, because other passages of Josephus were altered by Christian copyists, he cannot be "perfectly confident regarding its genuineness".

Schürer (1890) reports coins inscribed, in Greek, "of Herod the tetrarch", some bearing the name Tiberias, the latest of his forty-third year, which he dates to AD 39–40; like his father's, they carry no image.

first.text: The Gospels: John had told Herod his marriage to his brother's wife was unlawful; Herodias's grudge and the birthday oath brought his death.

second.text: Josephus: Herod feared John's influence might lead to a rebellion and put him to death at Macherus as a precaution (Antiquities 18.5.2).

first.text: Mark and Matthew: Herodias was "his brother Philip's wife".

second.text: Josephus: she was married to Herod, Herod the Great's son by Mariamne the high priest's daughter (Antiquities 18.5.1; 18.5.4). Whiston's translation adds "[Philip]" in brackets; the bracket is the translator's.

twoAccounts.topic: Did Herod himself want John dead?

first.text: Matthew: "when he would have put him to death, he feared the multitude".

second.text: Mark: Herodias "would have killed him; but she could not: For Herod feared John".

first.text: Antiquities 18.7.2: Gaius appointed "Lyons, a city of Gaul, to be his place of habitation".

second.text: War 2.9.6: he was banished "into Spain", and "Herod died in Spain, whither his wife had followed him".

views.label: Herod Philip, a different man from Philip the tetrarch
views.holders: Jamieson, Fausset and Brown (1871); G. F. Maclear (1877); H. A. W. Meyer (English 1880)

argument.text: They take Mark's "Philip" to be a son of Herod the Great, not the tetrarch, whom Josephus calls by the family name Herod. Jamieson, Fausset and Brown and Maclear call him "Herod Philip"; Meyer says Josephus's use of the name Herod "does not necessitate the supposition of a confusion".

views.label: Mark and Matthew made a mistake
views.holders: Schürer (1890), with Ewald, Keim and Volkmar

argument.text: Schürer holds that it would be strange for Josephus and the Gospels to choose different names for the same man, and for Herod to have two sons named Philip, and concludes that the two evangelists erred. He adds that the name in Luke 3:19, which the KJV's Greek text contains, ought to be struck out there.

questions.question: Where were John's prison and Herod's banquet?

views.label: Machaerus
views.holders: Schürer (1890), following Josephus

argument.text: Josephus names Macherus as the prison; Matthew and Mark assume the banquet was where John lay; Herod the Great had built a palace in the fortress, so the banquet may have been held there.

views.label: In Galilee, perhaps Tiberias
views.holders: Keim and Volkmar, as reported by Schürer (1890)

argument.text: They read Mark's guests, the "chief estates of Galilee", as placing the supper in Galilee. Schürer answers that the Gospels do not name the place.

views.label: At Julias
views.holders: Wieseler, as reported by Schürer (1890)

argument.text: Wieseler moved the scene to Julias; Schürer sees no reason for it.

views.label: A looser, popular use of "king"
views.holders: H. A. W. Meyer (English 1880), after Theophylact

argument.text: Matthew and Luke call him tetrarch, Mark "king Herod" (and Matthew too says "the king was sorry"). Meyer calls Mark's title "a more popular but less accurate term".

views.label: An inaccuracy
views.holders: Schürer (1890)

argument.text: Schürer says Matthew 14:1 and Luke 3:19 name him correctly and Mark 6:14 incorrectly calls him king.

notSaid: Scripture never uses the name Antipas; it calls him Herod.
The Gospels do not name the place where John was imprisoned and killed.
Scripture does not name the daughter of Herodias.
Scripture does not record how his rule ended.
Scripture does not say who the Herodians were (Matthew 22:16; Mark 3:6; 12:13), or how they were connected with him.
Scripture does not say why Pilate and Herod had been at enmity.

places.name: Galilee
places.note: His tetrarchy

places.name: Tiberias
places.note: The city he founded (Josephus)

places.name: Jerusalem
places.note: Where he questioned Jesus

places.name: Perea
places.note: The other half of his tetrarchy, by Josephus; Scripture says "beyond Jordan"; not in the atlas

places.name: Machaerus
places.note: John's prison and place of death, by Josephus (Antiquities 18.5.2); not in the atlas

places.name: Sepphoris
places.note: Walled by him, by Josephus (Antiquities 18.2.1); not in the atlas

places.name: Lyons, in Gaul
places.note: His place of banishment, by Josephus (Antiquities 18.7.2); not in the atlas

rulers.name: Philip the tetrarch
rulers.title: Tetrarch of Ituraea and Trachonitis, under Rome
rulers.tagline: Named once, in Luke's dating of John's preaching.

capital.name: Caesarea Philippi
capital.note: The town at Paneas he enlarged and named Caesarea (Josephus, Antiquities 18.2.1)

identifications.text: Luke names "his brother Philip tetrarch of Ituraea and of the region of Trachonitis", the brother of Herod the tetrarch of Galilee.

Josephus: Herod's will gave "Gaulonitis, and Trachonitis, and Paneas to Philip, who was his son" as a tetrarchy (Antiquities 17.8.1), and Augustus confirmed him in Batanea, Trachonitis, Auranitis and part of the house of Zenodorus (17.11.4).

He is a different man from the "Philip" whose wife Herodias had been (Mark 6:17): Josephus says Philip the tetrarch married Herodias's daughter Salome (Antiquities 18.5.4). Schürer (1890) and Jamieson, Fausset and Brown (1871) keep the two apart; the site has two person records.

dates.label: Scripture's numbers
dates.note: None. Luke names him in the fifteenth year of Tiberius (Luke 3:1).

dates.label: Schürer (1890)
dates.note: Tetrarch from 4 BC; died in the winter of AD 33/34, in the twentieth year of Tiberius.

dates.label: Josephus
dates.note: He died "in the twentieth year of the reign of Tiberius, after he had been tetrarch ... thirty-seven years" (Antiquities 18.4.6).

scriptureSays.text: "In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar", when John began to preach, Philip, Herod's brother, was "tetrarch of Ituraea and of the region of Trachonitis".
This is the only verse that names him. Scripture records no word or deed of his, and no meeting with Jesus.

accession.text: Herod's last will named Philip tetrarch (Antiquities 17.8.1); Augustus confirmed it, with a tribute of one hundred talents (Antiquities 17.11.4).

claim.text: Augustus confirmed his tetrarchy in the north-east (Antiquities 17.11.4).
"When Philip also had built Paneas, a city at the fountains of Jordan, he named it Caesarea" (Antiquities 18.2.1).
He raised the village of Bethsaida on the lake to a city and named it Julias after Caesar's daughter (Antiquities 18.2.1).
Luke names him among the rulers when John's preaching began.
He died at Julias and was buried "with great pomp" in a monument he had built; Tiberius added his principality to the province of Syria (Antiquities 18.4.6).

worship.text: Schürer (1890) reports that Philip's coins carry the heads of Augustus and Tiberius and a temple, which he takes to be Herod's temple of Augustus at Paneas, the first likeness of an emperor on the coins of a Jewish prince; he explains it by a population mainly not Jewish.

building.text: Caesarea at Paneas and Julias at Bethsaida (Antiquities 18.2.1).

alliances.text: He named both cities for the imperial family: Caesarea for Caesar, Julias for Caesar's daughter (Antiquities 18.2.1).

people.text: Josephus: "He had showed himself a person of moderation and quietness in the conduct of his life and government"; his judgment seat went with him on his journeys, and he heard complaints wherever he was (Antiquities 18.4.6).
Schürer (1890) describes the population of his tetrarchy as mixed, with the Syrian and Greek element prevailing.

claim.text: Luke dates his tetrarchy by "the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar", with Pontius Pilate governor of Judaea.

Josephus gives Philip a short obituary: thirty-seven years as tetrarch, a mild and accessible judge, death at Julias, burial in his own monument, and his territory added to Syria because "he left no sons behind him".
Schürer (1890) notes that the Paneas district had once belonged to the Iturean kingdom, so Luke's statement is "not altogether incorrect", though Ituraea proper, in the Lebanon, was never Philip's.

Schürer (1890) identifies the Gospels' Caesarea Philippi with the city Philip rebuilt at Paneas, but thought Philip's Bethsaida-Julias was probably a different place from the Bethsaida of the Gospels.

first.text: Luke: "tetrarch of Ituraea and of the region of Trachonitis".

second.text: Josephus: Gaulonitis, Trachonitis and Paneas (Antiquities 17.8.1); Batanea, Trachonitis, Auranitis and part of the house of Zenodorus (17.11.4); "Trachonitis and Gaulanitis, and of the nation of the Bataneans" (18.4.6). None of these lists names Ituraea.

questions.question: When was "the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius" (Luke 3:1)?

views.label: August AD 28 to August AD 29
views.holders: Schürer (1890)

argument.text: Schürer (1890) reckons Luke's fifteenth year as running from August AD 28 to August AD 29, and so dates John's first preaching then.

views.label: From late AD 25
views.holders: W. M. Ramsay (1898)

argument.text: Counted from the year when Tiberius first shared authority over the provinces with Augustus; Ramsay finds Luke's statements of time then consistent.

notSaid: Only Luke 3:1 names him; Scripture records no word or deed of his.
Scripture does not say that Philip built Caesarea Philippi; that is from Josephus.
The "Philip" whose wife Herodias had been (Mark 6:17) is, on most views, a different man.
Scripture does not say whether its Bethsaida is the town Philip renamed Julias.

places.name: Ituraea
places.note: Named by Luke

places.name: Trachonitis
places.note: Named by Luke

places.name: Caesarea Philippi
places.note: His city at Paneas (Josephus)

places.name: Bethsaida
places.note: Philip's Julias, by Josephus; whether the same as the Gospels' Bethsaida is debated

rulers.name: Herod Agrippa I
rulers.title: King over Judaea, under Rome
rulers.tagline: The king who killed James and imprisoned Peter.

capital.name: Jerusalem
capital.note: Josephus says he "loved to live continually at Jerusalem" (Antiquities 19.7.3)

identifications.text: Acts calls him only "Herod the king". He acts in Judaea, goes down "from Judaea to Caesarea", and dies there. Acts never calls him Agrippa and does not say whose son he was.
Josephus tells of Agrippa, Herod the Great's grandson, to whom Claudius added "Judea and Samaria" (Antiquities 19.5.1), and who died at Caesarea after his flatterers called him a god (19.8.2).
Schürer (1890) finds the principal points common to Acts and Josephus: Caesarea as the scene, the brilliant robe, the flattering shout and the sudden death.
Schürer (1890): "The New Testament, Acts xii., names him simply as Herod. By Josephus, however, and on the coins, he is always designated Agrippa."
Eusebius (about AD 325) heads his chapter on Acts 12 "Agrippa, who was also called Herod" (Church History 2.10).
He is not the "Herod the tetrarch" of Acts 13:1, the verse after his story ends; that is Herod Antipas.

dates.label: Scripture's numbers
dates.note: None. Acts sets his persecution "about that time", after the famine foretold for "the days of Claudius Caesar" (Acts 11:28; 12:1).

dates.label: Schürer (1890)
dates.note: King of Philip's former tetrarchy from AD 37, of Antipas's from about AD 40, of Judaea and Samaria from AD 41; died at Caesarea in AD 44.

dates.label: Josephus
dates.note: He died "in the fifty-fourth year of his age, and in the seventh year of his reign; for he reigned four years under Caius Caesar ... and he reigned, besides those, three years under the reign of Claudius Caesar" (Antiquities 19.8.2).

scriptureSays.text: "Herod the king stretched forth his hands to vex certain of the church. And he killed James the brother of John with the sword."

"Because he saw it pleased the Jews, he proceeded further to take Peter also", in "the days of unleavened bread". He set four quaternions of soldiers to guard him, "intending after Easter to bring him forth to the people".
The KJV's "Easter" in Acts 12:4 translates the same Greek word it renders "Passover" in Luke 22:1.

The church prayed without ceasing. On the night before Herod would have brought him out, an angel freed Peter, who said, "the Lord hath sent his angel, and hath delivered me out of the hand of Herod".
"When Herod had sought for him, and found him not, he examined the keepers, and commanded that they should be put to death." Then he went down from Judaea to Caesarea.
He "was highly displeased with them of Tyre and Sidon"; through Blastus, "the king's chamberlain", they asked for peace, "because their country was nourished by the king's country".

"Upon a set day Herod, arrayed in royal apparel, sat upon his throne, and made an oration". The people shouted, "It is the voice of a god, and not of a man." "And immediately the angel of the Lord smote him, because he gave not God the glory: and he was eaten of worms, and gave up the ghost."
"But the word of God grew and multiplied."

accession.text: Imprisoned at Rome under Tiberius, he was freed by the new emperor Gaius, who "put a diadem upon his head, and appointed him to be king of the tetrarchy of Philip. He also gave him the tetrarchy of Lysanias" (Antiquities 18.6.10).
Gaius later gave him the tetrarchy of Herod Antipas as well (Antiquities 18.7.2).
Claudius confirmed his kingdom and added "Judea and Samaria", "as due to his family", with Abila of Lysanias (Antiquities 19.5.1).

claim.text: Gaius made him king of Philip's former tetrarchy and Lysanias's (Antiquities 18.6.10).
Gaius added the tetrarchy of Antipas after banishing him (Antiquities 18.7.2).
Claudius added Judaea and Samaria (Antiquities 19.5.1).
He hung the golden chain Gaius had given him in the temple, over the treasury, as a memorial (Antiquities 19.6.1).
He began to strengthen the walls of Jerusalem's new quarter until Claudius, warned by Marcus the governor of Syria, ordered him to stop (Antiquities 19.7.2).
He killed James the brother of John with the sword.
He imprisoned Peter at the Passover season; an angel freed him; the keepers were put to death.
Tyre and Sidon sought peace with him through Blastus.
Hailed as a god after his oration, he was smitten by the angel of the Lord and died.

worship.text: He seized Peter because "he saw it pleased the Jews".

Josephus: "he loved to live continually at Jerusalem, and was exactly careful in the observance of the laws of his country"; "nor did any day pass over his head without its appointed sacrifice" (Antiquities 19.7.3).
On his return he offered all the sacrifices the law required and "ordained that many of the Nazarites should have their heads shorn" (Antiquities 19.6.1).

building.text: The walls of Jerusalem's new quarter, halted by Claudius (Antiquities 19.7.2); at Berytus a theatre, amphitheatre, baths and porticoes (Antiquities 19.7.5).

alliances.text: He entertained five client kings at Tiberias until Marcus, the governor of Syria, sent them home (Antiquities 19.8.1).
Tyre and Sidon depended on "the king's country" for food and sought peace with him.

people.text: At Caesarea "the people gave a shout, saying, It is the voice of a god, and not of a man."

Josephus says the multitude sat in sackcloth praying for him as he lay dying (Antiquities 19.8.2), but that at news of his death the people of Caesarea and Sebaste reviled him and feasted (Antiquities 19.9.1).

claim.text: Gaius made him king (Antiquities 18.6.10) and Claudius added Judaea and Samaria (19.5.1).
Acts sets his persecution "about that time", after Agabus foretold a dearth "which came to pass in the days of Claudius Caesar".

rulers.name: Blastus
rulers.note: the king's chamberlain, through whom they sought peace

claim.text: The two cities sought peace "because their country was nourished by the king's country".

At games in Caesarea for Caesar's safety, he entered the theatre on the second day wearing "a garment made wholly of silver"; flatterers called him a god and "the king did neither rebuke them, nor reject their impious flattery". He saw an owl above his head, was seized with pain in his belly, and died five days later.

Josephus says that years before, when Agrippa stood chained at Rome, a German prisoner saw an owl settle on the tree he leaned on and foretold his rise, and his death when he should see the bird again (Antiquities 18.6.7).

Eusebius admires "the account of Josephus for its agreement with the divine Scriptures", but his quotation reads that the king "saw an angel sitting above his head" where our Josephus has an owl (Church History 2.10.2, 6).

first.text: Acts: on a set day, in royal apparel on his throne, he "made an oration unto them" (after the embassy from Tyre and Sidon); the people cried "the voice of a god"; "immediately the angel of the Lord smote him, because he gave not God the glory: and he was eaten of worms".

second.text: Josephus: at games for Caesar, in a silver robe in the theatre, he let flatterers call him a god; he saw an owl, felt violent pains in his belly, and died after five days, aged fifty-four (Antiquities 19.8.2).

questions.question: Why does Eusebius's quotation of Josephus have an angel where Josephus has an owl?

views.label: Eusebius altered the text to match Acts
views.holders: "most writers on Eusebius", as reported by A. C. McGiffert (1890), who does not accept it

argument.text: McGiffert reports that many have accused Eusebius of wilfully changing Josephus's owl into an angel to confirm Acts.

views.label: Eusebius's copy of Josephus already read so
views.holders: J. B. Lightfoot, as quoted by A. C. McGiffert (1890), who agrees

argument.text: Lightfoot argues that the Greek words for the owl and the rope had dropped out of some copies, leaving "angel" (the same Greek word as "messenger"), so the change need not be dishonest.

questions.question: When in AD 44 did he die?

views.label: Spring of 44, at games for Claudius
views.holders: Schürer (1890)

argument.text: Schürer reads Acts as placing his death soon after the Passover of Peter's arrest; Josephus's festival, "celebrated to make vows for his safety" (Caesar's), was, Schürer argues, a special one held in the provinces after Claudius's return from Britain in the spring of 44. The regular games at Caesarea fell in 43.

views.label: 6 August 44, at the regular games founded by Herod
views.holders: Wieseler, followed by A. C. McGiffert (1890)

argument.text: McGiffert thinks the festival was more probably the five-yearly games Herod the Great instituted for Augustus, and gives Wieseler's date of 6 August 44.

notSaid: Acts never calls him Agrippa, and does not say whose son or grandson he was.
Acts does not say why he was displeased with Tyre and Sidon.
Acts gives no year for his death.
Josephus's account of him says nothing of James the brother of John, of Peter, or of the church.

places.name: Jerusalem
places.note: Where he killed James and imprisoned Peter (Acts 12 does not name the city)

places.name: Judaea
places.note: He went down "from Judaea" (Acts 12:19); his kingdom, by Josephus

places.name: Caesarea
places.note: Where he died

places.name: Tyre
places.note: Sought peace with him

places.name: Sidon
places.note: Sought peace with him

places.name: Trachonitis
places.note: Part of Philip's former tetrarchy, his first kingdom (Josephus)

places.name: Galilee
places.note: Antipas's former tetrarchy, added by Gaius (Josephus)

places.name: Abilene
places.note: Lysanias's former tetrarchy, given to him (Josephus, Antiquities 18.6.10)

rulers.name: Agrippa II
otherNames: Marcus Julius Agrippa (coins and inscriptions, by Schürer)
rulers.title: King under Rome, of lands north and east of Galilee
rulers.tagline: The king who heard Paul's defence at Caesarea.

capital.name: Caesarea Philippi
capital.note: Enlarged by him and renamed Neronias for Nero (Josephus, Antiquities 20.9.4); Schürer calls it his capital

identifications.text: Acts calls him "king Agrippa" and sets him beside Bernice in the time of the governor Festus. Acts never calls him Herod and does not say who his father was.

Josephus: Agrippa, son of King Agrippa, was seventeen when his father died (Antiquities 19.9.1); Claudius later gave him Philip's former tetrarchy (20.7.1); his sister Bernice, widowed by the death of her uncle and husband Herod, king of Chalcis, was the subject of a rumour about the two of them (20.7.3); and he was king while Festus was procurator (20.8.11).
Schürer (1890) places the visit of Acts 25:13 in AD 60, when Agrippa and Bernice came "with great pomp" to welcome the new procurator Festus.

Josephus names Bernice and Drusilla as daughters of Agrippa I (Antiquities 19.9.1), and says Drusilla, married to Azizus king of Emesa, left him to marry Felix (20.7.1–2): so the Drusilla of Acts 24:24, Felix's wife, was Agrippa II's sister.

dates.label: Schürer (1890)
dates.note: King of Chalcis from about AD 50; of Philip's former tetrarchy from AD 53, with parts of Galilee and Perea added by Nero; died in the third year of Trajan, AD 100, by the report of Justus of Tiberias preserved by Photius.

dates.label: Earlier death (before AD 93/94)
dates.note: Tillemont (1732), Grätz (1877) and others, as listed by Schürer, put his death before Josephus wrote his Life, which speaks of him as dead.

scriptureSays.text: "King Agrippa and Bernice came unto Caesarea to salute Festus." Festus laid Paul's case before him: a man "left in bonds by Felix", accused over questions "of one Jesus, which was dead, whom Paul affirmed to be alive".
Agrippa said, "I would also hear the man myself."

Next day Agrippa and Bernice came "with great pomp" into the place of hearing. Festus said he had "no certain thing to write unto my lord" and had brought Paul "specially before thee, O king Agrippa".

"Then Agrippa said unto Paul, Thou art permitted to speak for thyself." Paul called himself happy to answer before him, "because I know thee to be expert in all customs and questions which are among the Jews".

Paul told of his life as a Pharisee, his persecuting, the light and voice on the road to Damascus, and his preaching; he said, "the king knoweth of these things ... for this thing was not done in a corner."
"King Agrippa, believest thou the prophets? I know that thou believest. Then Agrippa said unto Paul, Almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian."

Rising with the governor and Bernice, they agreed, "This man doeth nothing worthy of death or of bonds", and Agrippa said to Festus, "This man might have been set at liberty, if he had not appealed unto Caesar."

accession.text: Claudius meant to give him his father's kingdom, but his advisers said it was too great for so young a man (Antiquities 19.9.2).
When his uncle Herod, king of Chalcis, died, "Claudius Caesar bestowed his dominions on Agrippa, junior" (Antiquities 20.5.2).
Claudius then gave him "the tetrarchy of Philip and Batanea, and added thereto Trachonites, with Abila", taking Chalcis back (Antiquities 20.7.1).
Nero added part of Galilee, Tiberias and Tarichae, and Julias in Perea with fourteen villages (Antiquities 20.8.4).

claim.text: Claudius gave him his uncle's kingdom of Chalcis (Antiquities 20.5.2).
He exchanged Chalcis for Philip's former tetrarchy and Abila (Antiquities 20.7.1).
Nero gave him Tiberias, Tarichae and Julias (Antiquities 20.8.4).
With Bernice he greeted Festus and heard Paul's defence.
He built a dining room in the palace at Jerusalem overlooking the temple; the Jews built a wall to block the view, and Nero let it stand (Antiquities 20.8.11).
When the high priest Ananus had James stoned, "king Agrippa took the high priesthood from him" (Antiquities 20.9.1).
He enlarged Caesarea Philippi and named it Neronias in Nero's honour (Antiquities 20.9.4).
He urged the people of Jerusalem not to war with Rome; when the revolt came, the rebels burned "the palaces of Agrippa and Bernice" (War 2.16.4–5; 2.17.6).

worship.text: Schürer (1890): with Chalcis he received the oversight of the temple and the right to appoint the high priests, which he used repeatedly until the war (Antiquities 20.1.3; 20.8.11; 20.9.1).

Josephus reports that the high priest Ananus, between governors, had "the brother of Jesus, who was called Christ, whose name was James" stoned, and that Agrippa removed him after three months (Antiquities 20.9.1).

building.text: Caesarea Philippi enlarged as Neronias; a theatre at Berytus with yearly shows (Antiquities 20.9.4).

alliances.text: He came to Caesarea to greet the new governor Festus, who consulted him about Paul.
Schürer (1890): through the war of 66–70 he stood on the Roman side; he hosted Vespasian at Caesarea Philippi and was with Titus.

people.text: Bernice sat with him at Paul's hearing and rose with him and the governor.
Josephus reports a rumour about Bernice and her brother, which she sought to disprove by marrying Polemon, king of Cilicia, a marriage that did not last (Antiquities 20.7.3).

Suetonius writes of Titus's "notorious passion for queen Berenice, to whom it was even said that he promised marriage", and that as emperor he sent her from Rome "against her will and against his own" (Titus 7).

rulers.name: Nero
rulers.note: never named in Scripture; by date, the "Caesar" and "Augustus" of Acts 25

claim.text: Claudius gave him Chalcis and then Philip's former tetrarchy (Antiquities 20.5.2; 20.7.1). Nero, who had sent Festus to succeed Felix (20.8.9), added Tiberias, Tarichae and Julias (20.8.4).
Festus had come "into Felix' room" and inherited Paul as a prisoner; he laid the case before Agrippa.
Josephus says Agrippa read his history of the war and "wrote me sixty-two letters, and attested to the truth of what I had therein delivered" (Life 65).
Schürer (1890) notes that the genuineness of Josephus's sentence on James, "the brother of Jesus, who was called Christ", is seriously disputed.
Schürer (1890) reports coins of Agrippa bearing the names of Nero, Vespasian, Titus and Domitian; one of his thirty-fifth year shows him alive in AD 95 at least.
Suetonius, Titus 7: Titus's passion for "queen Berenice", and her dismissal from Rome when he became emperor.

questions.question: What did Agrippa mean by "Almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian" (Acts 26:28)?

views.label: Almost persuaded, and in earnest
views.holders: the KJV's rendering, following Chrysostom; J. A. Bengel (1742); John Gill (1746–1748); Jamieson, Fausset and Brown (1871)

argument.text: They read the words as a real admission that Paul had nearly won him; Bengel sees "a motion towards good in him", and Jamieson, Fausset and Brown argue that Paul's reply ("both almost, and altogether") suits only that sense.

views.label: "With little persuasion": a dismissive answer
views.holders: H. A. W. Meyer (English 1877–1879); C. J. Ellicott's commentary (about 1880); J. R. Lumby (1882)

argument.text: They hold that the Greek means "with little" (effort, words or time), not "almost", and read the reply as mockery: Ellicott calls it "a cynical sneer", and Lumby cites the Revised Version's "With but little persuasion thou wouldest fain make me a Christian".

views.label: AD 100
views.holders: Justus of Tiberias (as summarised by Photius), followed by Schürer (1890)

argument.text: Justus put his death in the third year of Trajan; Schürer sees no reason to doubt it, since his coins show him alive at least in AD 95 and Josephus's Life need not have been written straight after the Antiquities.

views.label: Before AD 93/94
views.holders: Tillemont (1732), Jost, Brann (1871), Grätz (1877) and Brüll (1885), as listed by Schürer

argument.text: They reject or emend Justus's date because Josephus's Life, which speaks of Agrippa as dead, was taken to have been written right after the Antiquities in AD 93 or 94.

notSaid: Acts never calls him Herod, and does not say whose son he was.
Acts does not say how Bernice was related to him; Josephus calls her his sister.
Acts records his words to Paul but says nothing of his faith beyond them.
Josephus does not mention Paul.
